title: Test day five
hook: notice what you love: a boy steals pears he doesn't want, and Augustine learns what really moves a person
tomorrow: what was the world still missing on the seventh day?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: skipped. The parts of the rule you slid past, noticed without a lecture. Today, the other end of the test: the part you'd miss if it were gone.

Some songs you skip after a few seconds. One song you play again before it's even over, and nobody has to make you. Now a night in North Africa, long ago. Late one night, a teenage boy and his friends shake down a pear tree near his family's vineyard. The pears aren't even good. They take a few bites and throw the rest to the pigs. Years later, that boy, Augustine, still can't stop asking why he did it.
screen: `A SONG YOU REPLAY.` → `A PEAR TREE AT NIGHT.` → `WHY DID HE DO IT?`

segments.voice: He tells the story in his Confessions, a long book spoken to God. His answer surprises him. He didn't love the pears. He loved the stealing, and the friends he did it with; alone, he says, he would never have done it. His answer grows into a teaching that runs through the whole book: a person is moved by what they love. Later in the same book he puts it in four Latin words: pondus meum amor meus. My weight is my love. A stone falls down, fire rises up, each toward its place, and love, he says, is the pull that carries a person wherever they go. For Augustine, the trouble is rarely that we love nothing. It's that our loves are out of order. In another book he calls virtue the right ordering of love. So the change he hoped for wasn't more willpower. It was loving better things, and loving them in a better order. Day five of a test is a good day to borrow him. By day five, effort alone can wear thin. What you love keeps pulling. If one part of your rule is the song you'd replay, it isn't a luxury. It's the weight, and it may carry the rest.
screen: `A PEAR TREE, AND A QUESTION.` · `HE LOVED THE STEALING, AND THE FRIENDS.` · `MY WEIGHT IS MY LOVE.` · `LOVES IN THE RIGHT ORDER.` · then, large: `WHAT YOU LOVE CARRIES THE REST.`

segments.voice: Go back over the five days of your test, slowly, one part of the rule at a time. For each part, ask only this: did I love it, or only do it? Then say the name of the one you'd miss most, out loud, once, and let your hands rest while it comes back to mind.
Test day five: the day you notice which part of your rule you love. Augustine's word for that pull is pondus, weight.
For the road: loved, the weight that carries the rest of the rule. That's day 1695.

screen: `DAY 1695 COUNTS.` → `YOUR RULE · 7 OF 12.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT WAS THE WORLD STILL MISSING ON THE SEVENTH DAY?`

howItsDone: Augustine tells the pear theft in book two of his Confessions, and in City of God he calls virtue the order of love. On a personal rule, a test week can include a short note of the part kept gladly, not only the parts kept.
